--- title: "Predicting High-Risk Buildings in Philadelphia" subtitle: "From Reactive Inspections to Risk-Based Prioritization" author: "Liz Crouse, Shaurya Chauhan, Arzoo Gupta" date: "April 28, 2026" format: revealjs: theme: serif slide-number: true progress: true transition: fade transition-speed: fast fig-align: center fig-width: 9 fig-height: 6 execute: echo: false warning: false message: false editor: visual --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The Problem: A Reactive Inspection System Philadelphia's building inspection system is driven by **complaints**, not risk: - Only **\~7%** of rental units inspected annually *(Pew Charitable Trusts, 2021)* - Fewer than **45 inspectors** citywide *(Pew, 2021)* - Complaint-driven system → **systematic underreporting** in vulnerable communities *(Urban Institute, 2022)* - All buildings treated **equally** despite highly **unequal risk** > The city lacks a systematic way to prioritize which buildings need inspection most. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Why This Matters: Inspection Results {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](presentation_final_v2_files/figure-revealjs/result-distribution-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: These results show that only a small share of inspections fail (\~5%). However, these failures are not random—they cluster and follow patterns. → Opportunity to prioritize inspections based on risk. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Failure Rates Vary by Certification Type ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](presentation_final_v2_files/figure-revealjs/cert-type-results-1.png){fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: Certification type is an important control—we account for this in the model. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The Data: Five Sources Joined at the Block Group {.scrollable .smaller} | Source | What it contributes | |------------------------------------|------------------------------------| | **L&I Building Certifications** | Outcome variable: pass / fail; certification type fixed effects | | **OPA Property Data** | Market value, age, property count — split by SF / MF / commercial land use | | **311 Fire Complaints** | Fire department request volume per block group — early warning signal | | **Census ACS 2022** | Median income, vacancy rate, % renter-occupied, rent burden | | **Spatial distances** | Distance to nearest inspection (`avg_dst_nr_`), transit, city center | Each **property-level** observation is enriched by its surrounding **block group context**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Where Do Failures Cluster? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](presentation_final_v2_files/figure-revealjs/failure-map-1.png){fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Modeling Approach: Iterative Logistic Regression {.scrollable .smaller} **Why logistic regression?** Binary outcome (fail/pass), interpretable odds ratios, handles continuous + categorical predictors and interaction terms. | Model | Key change | Issue found | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | Model 1 | Distance features only, imbalanced data | Near-zero sensitivity — almost no failures predicted | | Model 2 | \+ ACS features + interactions | Still imbalanced | | Model 3 | \+ `upSample()` + threshold lowered to 0.3 | Sensitivity 94% but specificity only 35% | | Model 4 | \+ `bldngcrtt` fixed effects, threshold scan (sensitivity ≥ 0.80) | Near-final | | **Final** | Dropped noise variables, kept 4 key interactions | **AUC = 0.802** | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Final Model Predictors and Key Interactions {.smaller} ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **What we capture** - **Spatial risk** - Proximity to other inspections\ - Distance to transit and city center - **Neighborhood context** - Vacancy rate\ - Income and rent burden\ - Share of renter-occupied housing ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Behavioral & environmental signals** - 311 complaint activity\ - Property characteristics (age, value, density)\ - Certification type (controls for inspection differences) **Key idea** - Risk is shaped by how these factors interact — not any single variable ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What Drives Failure? Odds Ratios ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](presentation_final_v2_files/figure-revealjs/odds-ratios-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Handling Class Imbalance and Threshold Selection {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](presentation_final_v2_files/figure-revealjs/threshold-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: ::: smaller We selected a threshold that prioritizes identifying unsafe buildings. This ensures we capture most high-risk properties, even if it means inspecting some low-risk ones. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Final Model Performance ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Metric Value Interpretation
AUC 0.803 Good discrimination — model meaningfully separates high and low risk properties
Sensitivity 0.803 Catches 81% of actual failures — meets our target for a triage tool
Specificity 0.646 Correctly clears 63% of safe buildings — reduces unnecessary inspections
NPV 0.987 If model says safe, it is correct 99% of the time — key for prioritization
Threshold 0.420 Tuned to prioritize recall over precision given the cost of missed failures
````` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Where Does the Model Struggle? Residual Map ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](presentation_final_v2_files/figure-revealjs/residual-map-1.png){fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Limitations and Bias {.scrollable .smaller} **The training data reflects enforcement, not true risk**\ The model learns from where the city *already* inspects—complaint-driven neighborhoods are overrepresented. It captures enforcement patterns, not underlying building conditions. **Underreporting compounds over time**\ Vulnerable communities call 311 less → lower predicted risk → fewer inspections → continued under-enforcement. The `Pct_Renter_Occupied × log_n_requests` interaction captures this partially but does not resolve it. **Certification type dominates (OR = 3.66)**\ Sprinkler inspections fail at 3.7× the baseline rate. This is a legitimate control variable but means the model is partly predicting *what kind of inspection was scheduled*, not just building condition. **Residual spatial autocorrelation**\ Moran's I on residuals shows remaining spatial structure, suggesting spatial cross-validation and additional spatial features as clear next steps. > **This is a decision-support tool. It should inform inspector deployment, not replace human judgment.** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Implementation and Safeguards {.scrollable .smaller} **How the city uses this:** 1. Run final model on all L&I-registered properties periodically 2. Assign predicted failure probability (0–1) to each building 3. Sort into risk tiers (High / Medium / Low) by district 4. Produce prioritized inspection lists for field staff 5. Retrain quarterly as new inspection outcomes accumulate **Required safeguards:** - Human oversight: scores inform, not replace, inspector decisions - Equity audits by census tract: monitor for systematic over/under-prediction in lower-income areas - Transparent methodology: public documentation and grievance process - Model monitoring: flag degradation in cross-validated AUC over time ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## References {.smaller} **Data Sources** - Philadelphia Department of Licenses & Inspections - Building Certifications (OpenDataPhilly) - City of Philadelphia Office of Property Assessment - `opa_properties_public.geojson` - Philadelphia 311 Service Requests - Fire Department calls (OpenDataPhilly) - U.S. Census Bureau - American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates, 2022, block group level **References** - Pew Charitable Trusts (2021). *Philadelphia's Rental Housing Challenge.* - Urban Institute (2022). *Who Is Left Behind by Complaint-Based Code Enforcement?* - National Low Income Housing Coalition (2022). *Out of Reach: The High Cost of Housing.* **R Packages** `tidyverse` · `sf` · `tidycensus` · `tigris` · `caret` · `pROC` · `spdep` · `kableExtra`

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
